title: ABRAHAM LIVED 38 YEARS AFTER SARAH DIED—BUT WHAT HAPPENED IN THOSE YEARS REVEALS SOMETHING MOST BELIEVERS OVERLOOK
paragraphs: ABRAHAM LIVED 38 YEARS AFTER SARAH DIED—BUT WHAT HAPPENED IN THOSE YEARS REVEALS SOMETHING MOST BELIEVERS OVERLOOK

He buried the woman who had walked beside him through decades of waiting, disappointment, miracles, and impossible promises. But God was not finished writing Abraham’s story. And what happened after Sarah's death carries a powerful message for anyone who has ever buried a dream, lost someone they loved, or wondered whether their best days were already behind them.
There is something heartbreaking about realizing that the person who witnessed your greatest miracle may not be there to witness the rest of your journey.
Imagine Abraham standing beside Sarah’s grave.
The woman who had followed him into the unknown was gone.
The woman who had laughed when God promised her a son in her old age was gone.
The woman who had waited through years of barrenness, uncertainty, disappointment, and divine silence was gone.
The woman who finally held Isaac—the child whose very existence testified that God keeps His promises—was gone.
And Abraham was still alive.
Still breathing.
Still carrying promises.
Still walking with the God who had called him out of his homeland so many years earlier.
But now there was an empty place beside him.
And here is the question that makes this story more than a historical curiosity:
How many years did Abraham live after Sarah died—and what did God do with those remaining years?
The answer is 38 years.
But if you stop at the number, you will miss the beauty hidden between two graves.
Because the Bible does not merely tell us when Abraham died.
It shows us something remarkable about what faith looks like when one chapter closes, grief becomes part of your story, and God still has more to accomplish.
And somewhere in those 38 years, there is a message for the person reading this who has quietly wondered:
“Lord, is there still anything left for me?”
Genesis 23:1 records Sarah’s age at death:
“And Sarah was an hundred and seven and twenty years old: these were the years of the life of Sarah.” (KJV)
Sarah died at 127 years old.

Genesis 17:17 establishes that Abraham was ten years older than Sarah. When God spoke of the promised son, Abraham asked whether a child could be born to a man who was a hundred years old and whether Sarah, who was ninety, could bear.
That ten-year difference matters.
When Sarah died at 127, Abraham was approximately 137.
Then Genesis 25:7 tells us:
“And these are the days of the years of Abraham's life which he lived, an hundred threescore and fifteen years.” (KJV)
Abraham died at 175.
Subtract 137 from 175.
Thirty-eight years.
Thirty-eight more years of life after Sarah's death.
Thirty-eight years after the funeral.
Thirty-eight years after the tears.
Thirty-eight years after the woman who shared so much of his extraordinary journey was laid to rest.
And perhaps the most surprising thing is this:
Abraham's story did not end when Sarah's earthly story ended.
But before we explore those remaining years, we need to stand with Abraham at the place where his grief became visible.
Genesis 23:2 says:
“And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.”
Do not rush past those words.
Abraham wept.
The man who believed God's promise wept.
The man who left his homeland in obedience to God wept.
The man whose faith would later be celebrated in Hebrews 11 wept.
The man who had seen God do the impossible still knew what it meant to experience unbearable loss.
Faith did not make him incapable of grief.
Trusting God did not make him emotionally untouchable.
Receiving a miracle did not mean he would never experience sorrow again.
He was a man of faith.
And he was a grieving husband.
Both were true.
Some Christians have quietly absorbed the idea that strong faith means never breaking down, never questioning, never feeling devastated.
But Scripture never teaches that godly people are incapable of tears.
Abraham's tears were not evidence that he had abandoned his faith.
They were evidence that he had loved.
And there is something profoundly comforting about a Bible that does not erase the tears of its heroes.
Maybe you understand Abraham more than you expected.
Maybe you have buried someone whose voice you still remember.
Maybe you still reach for your phone before remembering that the person you want to call is no longer there.
Maybe you have walked into a room and felt the weight of an empty chair.
Or perhaps the thing you buried was not a person.
Perhaps it was a marriage you desperately wanted to save.
A relationship that ended despite your prayers.
A business that collapsed after years of sacrifice.
A ministry that never became what you hoped.
A dream that seemed so certain until life turned in another direction.
And somewhere along the way, you began to confuse the death of one chapter with the death of your entire purpose.
But Abraham's remaining 38 years remind us of something important:
The end of a precious season does not necessarily mean the end of God's work in your life.
That does not mean grief is easy.
It does not mean every loss will be replaced.
And it certainly does not mean that God owes us another 38 years or another earthly miracle.
It means that as long as we remain in His hands, our lives are not reduced to the worst thing that has happened to us.
Now look carefully at what Abraham did after Sarah died.
Genesis 23 describes him purchasing a burial place from Ephron the Hittite.
He paid four hundred shekels of silver for the field and the cave of Machpelah.
This was not merely an emotional detail about arranging a funeral.
It carried covenant significance.
God had promised Abraham the land of Canaan.
Yet Abraham spent much of his life living there as a sojourner.
He possessed the promise of an inheritance from God, but he did not personally possess the fullness of that inheritance during his lifetime.
When Sarah died, Abraham purchased a burial place in the very land God had promised to his descendants.
Consider the painful beauty of that moment.
The man who had been promised a land was purchasing a grave in it.
The man who had been promised descendants beyond counting was burying the mother of the promised son.
The man who had received extraordinary promises was still living in a world where death was painfully real.
And yet God's covenant had not failed.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 23:4 records Abraham describing himself as:
גֵּר־וְתוֹשָׁב (gēr wĕtôshāv)
The expression means a resident foreigner or sojourner and settler.
Abraham was acknowledging his position among the people of the land.
He lived there, but he did not yet possess the inheritance in its fullness.
That is not a small detail.
It helps us understand the nature of biblical faith.
Faith is not always standing in the middle of everything God has promised and celebrating its complete fulfillment.
Sometimes faith is standing beside a grave, holding a promise whose final fulfillment you will not see in your earthly lifetime.
Hebrews 11:13 says of the faithful:
“These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them...” (KJV)
Abraham did not see every covenant promise fulfilled before his death.
Yet he trusted the God who had spoken.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to confront us.
Because many of us have been taught to celebrate faith when the doors open, the healing comes, the money arrives, the relationship is restored, and the answer appears.
But what about faith when you are still waiting?
What about faith when the person you prayed for dies?
What about faith when you obey God and still experience disappointment?
What about faith when your hands are empty but His Word remains true?
Abraham's life teaches us that the reliability of God's promises cannot be measured only by how much we personally experience before we die.
The God who made the covenant was faithful even when Abraham's earthly life remained incomplete.
And this is where we must be careful.
God's promises to Abraham were specific covenant promises. We should not turn them into guarantees that every believer will receive land, wealth, children, marriage, or long life.
But through Jesus Christ, believers have something even greater than the assurance of favorable earthly circumstances.
We have the promise of eternal life in Him.
We have forgiveness through His blood.
We have the hope of resurrection.
And we have a Savior whose faithfulness does not expire when our circumstances become painful.
Now notice what Scripture records after Sarah's death.
Genesis 24 tells the remarkable story of Abraham arranging for a wife for Isaac.
Sarah was gone.
But the covenant promise was moving forward through the next generation.
Abraham instructed his servant not to take a wife for Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, but to go to his relatives.
The servant's journey led to Rebekah.
And Genesis 24:67 contains one of the tenderest details in the entire account.
Isaac brought Rebekah into Sarah's tent, took her as his wife, loved her, and was comforted after his mother's death.
Read that carefully.
Isaac had lost his mother.
And Scripture does not pretend that the promised son was immune to sorrow.
Even the child born through a miracle experienced grief.
Yet the next generation continued.
The covenant family continued.
God's purposes continued.
Not because Sarah was unimportant.
Not because Abraham could replace her.
But because God's covenant faithfulness was greater than the lifespan of any one human being.
Sarah's death did not cancel the promise God had made concerning Isaac.
That truth is especially powerful for parents and grandparents.
You may not live to see every prayer answered for your children.
You may not witness every spiritual battle they will face.
You may never know the full influence of your obedience.
But your responsibility is not to control the generations after you.
It is to be faithful to God with the time entrusted to you.
The results belong to Him.
And then comes a detail that surprises many readers.
Genesis 25:1 says:
“Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.” (KJV)
Yes.
After Sarah's death, Abraham married again.
And Genesis 25:2 records six sons associated with that marriage: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
The Bible does not tell us everything about Abraham's relationship with Keturah.
It does not describe his emotional recovery.
It does not reveal exactly when the marriage took place.
It does not tell us that his love for Sarah disappeared.
And we should not invent those details.
What we can say is that Genesis records additional family life in Abraham's later years.
His household's story continued beyond Sarah's death.
This matters because grief can sometimes make people feel guilty for experiencing life again.
A widower may feel guilty for smiling.
A widow may feel guilty for enjoying another season.
Someone who has experienced devastating loss may wonder whether healing means betrayal.
But Scripture does not require the bereaved to remain permanently frozen in the moment of loss.
Love for someone who has died and gratitude for the life still before us are not necessarily enemies.
A new season does not erase the significance of an earlier one.
And yet this passage must not be turned into pressure.
Not every widow or widower needs to remarry.
Not everyone will have children.
Not everyone will experience a dramatic new beginning.
Abraham's later marriage is a historical detail in his life, not a universal command for grieving people.

The deeper truth is that God remains worthy of our trust in every season—whether He leads us into new relationships, quiet service, unexpected responsibilities, or a life that looks different from what we imagined.
There is another important detail in Genesis 25.
Verse 5 says:
“And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.” (KJV)
Verse 6 explains that Abraham also gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them eastward, away from Isaac, while he was still alive.
The distinction matters because Isaac remained the designated heir of the covenant line.
Abraham had other descendants, but God's particular covenant promise would continue through Isaac.
This was not simply a story about an elderly man accumulating possessions or expanding his family.
It was about the unfolding of a promise that ultimately pointed beyond Abraham himself.
And that brings us to the most important part of this entire account.
Because if we only admire Abraham, we have not yet reached the heart of the Gospel.
The story of Abraham is not ultimately about how remarkable Abraham was.
It is about how faithful God is.
Abraham was not a flawless hero.
He had moments of fear.
He had moments of weakness.
He made decisions that caused pain.
Genesis 12 and Genesis 20 record troubling episodes in which Abraham represented Sarah as his sister while withholding the truth about their marriage.
Genesis 16 records the painful consequences surrounding Hagar and Ishmael after Sarah and Abraham attempted to obtain a child through Hagar.
These were not examples of perfect faith.
They were reminders that even the people God uses are capable of serious failure.
And still, God's covenant purposes endured.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because Abraham's mistakes were righteous.
But because God's faithfulness was greater than Abraham's failures.
Here is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes deeply personal.
Abraham's story contains fear, deception, family conflict, painful consequences, and imperfect obedience.
Yet Scripture also remembers him as a man who believed God.
Genesis 15:6 says:
“And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is especially meaningful:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה (wĕheʾĕmin baYHWH)
“And he believed in the LORD.”
The verse continues with the idea that this faith was reckoned or counted to him as righteousness.
This is foundational to the New Testament's explanation of justification by faith.
Paul returns to Abraham in Romans 4 to show that righteousness is not earned by a perfect record of human achievement.
Romans 4:3 says:
“For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.” (KJV)
And Romans 4:5 explains that God justifies the ungodly and counts faith for righteousness.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It means that our acceptance before God is not purchased by a lifetime of flawless performance.
It rests upon His grace, received through faith.
And the full revelation of that grace is found in Jesus Christ.
Galatians 3:16 identifies Christ as the ultimate promised offspring through whom the blessing associated with Abraham's covenant reaches its fulfillment.
The promise was always moving toward something greater than Abraham could see.
Toward a Redeemer.
Toward the cross.
Toward the empty tomb.
Toward the One who would confront the deepest enemy facing every descendant of Adam.
Death itself.
Abraham buried Sarah.
Eventually, Abraham himself was buried.
But Jesus Christ entered death and rose again.
That is why Christian hope is not merely the hope of having more years.
It is the hope of belonging to the One who conquered the grave.
Jesus declared in John 11:25:
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” (KJV)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say believers would never attend funerals.
He did not say faithful families would never experience tragedy.
He did not say everyone who trusts Him would live to 175.
He promised something greater.
Resurrection life in Him.
That is the hope Abraham's story ultimately invites us to consider through the fuller revelation of Scripture.
Not simply how long we live.
But whom we trust with our lives.
And whom we trust when our lives on earth come to an end.
There is a beautiful phrase in Genesis 25:8 describing Abraham's death.
The Hebrew text includes:
בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה (bĕśêvāh ṭôvāh)
It conveys the idea of a good old age or good old age with gray hair.
The verse says in the King James Version:
“Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full of years; and was gathered to his people.”
The Hebrew expression translated “full of years” is associated with being full or satisfied; the word “years” is supplied in the English rendering to express the sense.
This description does not mean Abraham had lived without sorrow.
He had known infertility in his household.
He had known displacement.
He had known conflict.
He had known fear.
He had known family pain.
He had buried Sarah.
But at 175, Scripture describes the end of his earthly life as a good old age.
A life does not have to be painless to have been meaningful.
A life does not have to unfold exactly as expected to bear witness to God's faithfulness.
And a person does not need to accomplish everything imaginable to finish the work God entrusted to them.
Then Genesis 25:9 gives us another scene worth remembering.
Isaac and Ishmael buried their father.
Two sons whose family history had been marked by painful separation appeared together in the account of Abraham's burial.
Scripture does not tell us whether all the wounds between them were healed.
It does not record a reconciliation conversation.
We should not claim more than the text reveals.
But their presence together at their father's burial is a striking final detail.
And where was Abraham buried?
In the cave of Machpelah.
The same burial place he had purchased when Sarah died.
Genesis 25:10 says:
“There was Abraham buried, and Sarah his wife.” (KJV)
After 38 years of life beyond Sarah's death, Abraham's earthly remains were laid to rest in the same place.
The narrative that showed us a grieving husband purchasing a grave now closes with the husband buried beside his wife.
Thirty-eight years separated their deaths.
But the biblical account brings us back to the same burial place.
There is something deeply moving about that.
Not because the grave was the fulfillment of every promise.
Not because death had the final word.
But because the same God who had sustained Abraham through decades of waiting remained faithful throughout his life.
And the story of God's covenant did not end at Machpelah.
Isaac lived on.
The promised line continued.
Generations passed.
And in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
The One in whom God's redemptive purposes reach their fulfillment.
Now, consider a question that may be more important than the original question about Abraham's age.
What are you doing with the years God has given you?
Not the years you wish you could recover.
Not the years you imagine you should have had.
Not the years someone else has been given.
The life you have today.
Because none of us knows whether we have 38 more years.
Some will have decades.
Some will have only a little time.
That is not meant to frighten you into desperation.
It is meant to awaken you to the preciousness of the present.
Maybe you have been postponing repentance.
You keep telling yourself you will surrender that hidden sin when life becomes easier.
Maybe you have been delaying forgiveness.
You know bitterness is poisoning your heart, but you keep rehearsing what someone did to you.
Maybe you have been neglecting prayer.
Your Bible sits unopened while your soul grows exhausted.
Maybe you have been living under the weight of shame.
You believe Jesus can forgive other people, but somewhere deep inside you wonder whether your own failures have placed you beyond His mercy.
Listen carefully.
Abraham's righteousness was not grounded in his perfection.
And your hope of salvation is not grounded in yours.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we finally accumulated enough religious achievements to deserve His attention.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection is the declaration that sin and death do not have ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
That grace is not permission to remain comfortable in rebellion.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God instructs us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly lives.
Real grace does not merely soothe a guilty conscience.
It transforms the person who receives it.
It calls us out of hiding.
It brings our sin into the light.
It teaches us to turn from what is destroying us.
It leads us back to Christ.
And if you have been telling yourself that your story is too scandalous, your past too dirty, your mistakes too public, or your failures too deeply rooted, remember this:
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people have earned a reward.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died and rose again to save sinners who could never save themselves.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
It is the proper response to the mercy of God.
And perhaps this article found you in a season when you needed to hear that.
Perhaps you have lost someone.
Perhaps you are growing older and wondering whether your life still matters.
Perhaps you feel embarrassed that your faith has been weaker than you expected.
Perhaps you have been carrying a secret that nobody in your church knows about.
Or perhaps you have become so familiar with Christian language that you have forgotten what it means to be genuinely surrendered to Jesus.
Then do not simply admire Abraham's 38 remaining years.
Examine your own heart.
Are you trusting Christ?
Are you turning from sin?
Are you living in obedience to His Word?
Are you using the time entrusted to you to love God and love others?
Are you passing on truth to the people who will remain when your earthly journey ends?
And if you realize you have wandered far from Him, you do not have to manufacture a dramatic religious performance.
Come to Christ with sincerity.
Confess your sin.
Ask for mercy.
Trust in His finished work.
And follow Him.
You can begin with a simple prayer:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much of my life trying to control what only You can hold. I have carried regrets, hidden sins, disappointments, and fears. Forgive me. Teach me to trust You in the seasons I do not understand. Heal what is wounded in me. Correct what is sinful in me. Restore what has grown cold in my relationship with You. And help me live the rest of my days for Your glory, whether they are many or few. My hope is not in the number of years I have left, but in Your death and resurrection. Amen.”
And if this story has brought something painful or honest to the surface, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to reveal private details.
Sometimes a few sincere words can open the door to prayer, encouragement, and genuine Christian fellowship.
Someone else may be reading silently, wondering whether they can survive what they are facing.
Your testimony may remind them that they are not alone.
But there is something else I want to ask you.
Think of one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to condemn.
Someone you genuinely love.
A grieving parent.
A widow.
A struggling father.
A young believer who feels spiritually defeated.
A friend who has quietly stopped praying.
Someone who thinks their best years are gone.
A simple act of sharing cannot replace discipleship, prayer, or personal relationships, but it can place biblical encouragement in front of someone who might not otherwise encounter it.
Not because the words here are more important than Scripture, but because you may want to return to these passages when another difficult season comes.
And if you have been following Gospel Warrior, or have only recently discovered this community, I want you to understand something about why we continue this work.
We want to help people encounter Jesus Christ through the faithful teaching of Scripture.
Not merely collect religious quotations.
Not simply stir emotions for a moment.
But encourage real repentance, deeper biblical understanding, genuine spiritual growth, and lasting faithfulness to Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible to people who need it.
It can become part of your personal giving and generosity as you prayerfully consider how to steward what God has entrusted to you.

Scripture teaches the importance of supporting faithful ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or forced.
That balance matters.
It is not a payment for God's blessing.
It is not a replacement for your responsibilities to your local church, your family, or people in need.
And it should not be confused with a biblically mandated tithe.
But it can be a meaningful voluntary offering of support toward a ministry whose mission you believe is worth helping sustain.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is ministry.
It is the opportunity to keep placing Scripture before people who are hurting, questioning, repenting, searching, or learning to walk faithfully with Jesus.
You can still pray for this ministry.
You can still make use of the free resources.
Your financial situation does not determine your worth before God.
And the Gospel of Jesus Christ is not for sale.
If you are not, we are still grateful that you are here.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are encouraged to know Him, trust Him, and obey His Word.
Now, before you leave, return with me one last time to the cave of Machpelah.
Imagine the silence.
Sarah was buried there.
Thirty-eight years later, Abraham was buried there too.
Their earthly journeys had ended.
Their struggles were over.
Their years of waiting had passed.
And yet the promises of God continued unfolding long after both of them had died.
Abraham never saw Bethlehem.
He never stood beside the manger.
He never watched Jesus carry the cross.
He never saw the stone rolled away from the empty tomb.
But Jesus declared in John 8:56:
“Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.” (KJV)
Christ's words reveal that Abraham's hope reached toward the day of the Messiah, though Scripture does not explain every detail of what Abraham understood or saw.
The deepest significance of Abraham's faith was never confined to his lifespan.
It pointed toward Christ.
And that is the final lesson of those 38 years.
You can spend your life chasing a legacy that ends at your grave.
Or you can live by faith in the Savior whose kingdom will never end.
You can spend your remaining years consumed by what you have lost.
Or you can grieve honestly while learning to trust the Lord with what remains.
You can keep hiding behind your failures.
Or you can come into the light of the Gospel, repent, and receive the mercy offered through Jesus Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot guarantee tomorrow.
But today, you can turn to the One who holds eternity.
Abraham lived 38 years after Sarah died.
And those years remind us that God's faithfulness does not depend upon our ability to see the entire story.
The God who sustained Abraham through waiting, grief, weakness, and old age is the same God who has revealed His saving grace through Jesus Christ.
If your earthly story ended sooner than you expected, would your greatest confidence be in what you accomplished—or in the Savior who died and rose again for you?
And remember this:
The most important part of Abraham's final 38 years was not that he kept living after Sarah died, but that the God who held his promises was faithful long after Abraham himself was gone.
